akiec.name: Actinic Keratoses
akiec.description: A rough, scaly patch on the skin that develops from years of sun exposure. Represents early-stage precancerous skin damage.
akiec.cause: Accumulated UV exposure from the sun over many years.
akiec.cure: Treatments include cryotherapy, topical prescription creams, or photodynamic therapy. Close monitoring is recommended.

bcc.name: Basal Cell Carcinoma
bcc.description: Cancer that begins in the basal cells. It presents as a pearly or waxy bump and is the most common form of skin cancer.
bcc.cure: Surgical excision, topical medications, or localized radiation. Very high cure rate when caught early.

mel.name: Melanoma
mel.description: A serious form of skin cancer that begins in melanocytes. It can develop from an existing mole that changes rapidly.
mel.cause: Genetics and intense, intermittent UV exposure.
mel.cure: Surgical excision is the primary treatment. Advanced cases require immunotherapy or targeted therapy. Urgent consultation is required.

acne.name: Acne Vulgaris
acne.description: A condition occurring when hair follicles become plugged with oil and dead skin cells. In pigmented skin types, it often leaves post-inflammatory dark spots.
acne.cause: Hormones, overproduction of sebum, and bacterial overgrowth.
acne.cure: Topical retinoids, salicylic acid, antibiotics, or oral medications. Gentle skincare is vital to prevent scarring.

melasma.name: Melasma (Chloasma)
melasma.description: Common in brown or olive skin tones, presenting as symmetrical, irregular dark patches on the face (cheeks, bridge of nose, forehead).
melasma.cause: Hormonal shifts (e.g., pregnancy), sun exposure, and genetic predisposition.
melasma.cure: Strict, daily sun protection. Topical treatments involving hydroquinone, azelaic acid, or chemical peels given by dermatologists.

tinea_versicolor.name: Pityriasis Versicolor
tinea_versicolor.description: A fungal infection causing small, discolored patches of skin that can be lighter or darker than the surrounding skin. Common in hot, humid climates like India.
tinea_versicolor.cause: Overgrowth of Malassezia, a yeast naturally found on the skin.
tinea_versicolor.cure: Topical antifungal creams, lotions, or shampoos containing ketoconazole or selenium sulfide.

tinea_corporis.name: Ringworm (Tinea Corporis)
tinea_corporis.description: A fungal infection creating a ring-shaped, red, scaly rash with a clear center.
tinea_corporis.cause: Dermatophyte fungus spreading via direct contact with infected people, animals, or soil.
tinea_corporis.cure: Over-the-counter or prescription topical antifungal medications. Keep the area clean and dry.

vitiligo.name: Vitiligo
vitiligo.description: A condition causing the loss of skin pigment, resulting in clear, sharply demarcated white patches.
vitiligo.cause: Autoimmune condition where melanocytes are destroyed.
vitiligo.cure: Phototherapy, targeted topical corticosteroids or calcineurin inhibitors to manage and sometimes repigment patches.

pih.name: Post-Inflammatory Hyperpigmentation
pih.description: Darkened spots left behind after a skin injury, insect bite, or inflammation (like acne) heals. Very common in melanin-rich skin.
pih.cause: Excess melanin production linked to the skin's healing process.
pih.cure: Tyrosinase inhibitors (vitamin C, niacinamide, kojic acid), gentle exfoliation, and rigorous sun protection.

acanthosis_nigricans.name: Acanthosis Nigricans
acanthosis_nigricans.description: Thickened, velvety darkening of the skin, usually in folds and creases (neck, armpits). Often observed in metabolic syndromes.
acanthosis_nigricans.cause: Insulin resistance, obesity, or certain medications.
acanthosis_nigricans.cure: Managing underlying medical conditions (like metabolic syndrome or diabetes). Topical exfoliants can temporarily visually improve the area.

unknown.name: Unknown / Clear Skin
unknown.description: The AI could not confidently identify a specific pathological lesion.
unknown.cure: Maintain a healthy skincare routine and use SPF daily. If symptoms persist, seek professional medical advice.

nv.name: Melanocytic Nevus (Skin Mole)
nv.description: A common, benign skin lesion caused by a local proliferation of melanocytes. It typically presents as a regular, symmetric, and uniformly colored brown spot.
nv.cause: Genetics and sun exposure, especially during childhood.
nv.cure: Usually harmless and requires no treatment. Excision is recommended only if it exhibits rapid changes in size, shape, color, or causes symptoms.

bkl.name: Benign Keratosis (e.g. Seborrheic Keratosis)
bkl.description: A very common, non-cancerous skin growth that often looks waxy, scaly, or slightly raised, resembling a wart or a crusty brown patch.
bkl.cause: Natural aging, genetics, and cumulative sun exposure over time.
bkl.cure: Completely benign and requires no medical treatment. Can be removed for cosmetic reasons via cryotherapy, electrosurgery, or curettage.

df.name: Dermatofibroma
df.description: A common benign fibrous nodule, often found on the lower legs. It usually feels like a firm, hard lump just under the skin surface.
df.cause: Often arises following a minor skin injury or trauma, such as an insect bite, splinter, or thorn puncture.
df.cure: Benign and generally left alone. Complete surgical excision is an option if it becomes painful or cosmetically unacceptable.

vasc.name: Benign Vascular Lesion
vasc.description: A harmless condition characterized by dense collections of blood vessels near the skin surface, presenting as red or purple spots (e.g., cherry angiomas).
vasc.cause: Genetics, natural aging, and localized pooling or overgrowth of capillaries.
vasc.cure: No treatment is necessary. Can be successfully treated with vascular lasers or electrocautery if cosmetically bothersome or if they bleed easily.
